## 4. Load-test data (100,000 certificates)

```bash
npm run generate:east                      # takes ~3 s; can run while the server is up
npm run generate:east -- --count 250000    # other volumes
npm run generate:east -- --clear           # remove the generated rows
npm run generate:east -- --db /tmp/load.sqlite   # work on a separate database file instead
                                                 # (start the app on it with DB_PATH=/tmp/load.sqlite npm start)
```

The generator **does not modify the quick-start dataset**. The generated certificates belong to
their own 10 generated courses and 10,000 generated learners (flagged `is_generated = 1`) and are
numbered in a serial range of their own (`EAST-LT-0000001` …). The seeded tenants (their serial
counters included), admins, courses, learners, enrollments, certificates and audit events are left
exactly as they were - asserted row by row in the test suite - so `Safety 101`, `Alex Lee` and
every demo scenario behave as before, and the next certificate issued through the app is
`EAST-0000008` with or without the load-test data. Re-running the generator replaces the previous
generated set, so the count never piles up; `--clear` removes it and leaves exactly the rows that
were there without it; `npm run db:reset` restores the pristine dataset and shrinks the database
file back to its original size.

The generator writes everything in one transaction. While it runs, a server on the same database
keeps answering reads (which see the old rows until the generator commits) and retries of finished
bulk issues; new writes wait for it and complete as soon as it is done.

The data is built to contain many equal sort keys: ~2,500 distinct learner names for 100,000
certificates, 10 course titles, ~150 certificates per calendar day, and batches of 25 certificates
that share the exact same issue instant (like a real bulk issue). It is generated from a seeded
PRNG, so every run produces the same rows, serial numbers included (`--seed N` gives another set).

## 5. HTTP API

All endpoints except `/api/health` and `/api/actors` require `X-Actor-Email`. Errors have the shape
`{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}}`: `400` invalid input, `401` missing or unknown actor,
`404` unknown id (including ids of another tenant), `409` idempotency key reused for a different
request, `413` body larger than 100 kB, and `503` with `Retry-After` in two situations where
nothing was done and the request can simply be repeated: `database_busy` (another process has held
the database's write lock for longer than `DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS`) and `export_busy` (32 exports
are already waiting for a free export slot).

Query parameters are validated: an unknown value is a `400`, never silently ignored; a parameter
that is present but blank (`?sort=`) counts as not given. A few parameters also answer to a second
name (`q`/`search`, `sort`/`sortBy`, `order`/`dir`, `pageSize`/`limit`); sending two names of the
same parameter is a `400` as well, because one of them would have to be ignored. The one exception
is by design: the export has no pages and does not look at `page` and `pageSize`, so the query
string of a list request can be reused for the export of the same rows as it is.

| Method & path                              | Purpose |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------- |
| `GET /api/actors`                          | Seeded admins for the actor switcher (demo helper) |
| `GET /api/me`                              | The actor and tenant resolved from the header |
| `GET /api/certificates`                    | List. `q` (text contained in the learner name or serial number, case and accents ignored), `status` (`all`\|`active`\|`revoked`), `sort` (`issued`\|`learner`\|`course`\|`serial`\|`status`), `order` (`asc`\|`desc`), `page`, `pageSize` (≤ 100) |
| `GET /api/certificates/export.csv`         | CSV of everything matching the same `q`, `status`, `sort`, `order`. `HEAD` answers with the download's headers without running the export |
| `GET /api/certificates/:id`                | Detail incl. `issuedLocal`, `issuedUtcOffset` and `auditEvents` |
| `POST /api/certificates/:id/revoke`        | Revoke. Body `{"reason": "…"}` is optional. Idempotent |
| `GET /api/courses`                         | Courses of the tenant, by title |
| `GET /api/courses/:id/enrollments`         | Roster with per-learner eligibility and course totals, by learner name; `page`, `pageSize` (≤ 100) |
| `POST /api/bulk-issues`                    | Bulk issue. Body `{"courseId": 1}`, header `Idempotency-Key` |
| `GET /api/bulk-issues`, `GET /api/bulk-issues/:id` | Recent operations / the stored result of one |
| `GET /api/audit-events`                    | Audit trail; filters `certificateId`, `bulkOperationId`, `action` (`certificate.issued`\|`certificate.revoked`) |

Examples (with the default data):

```bash
A='X-Actor-Email: alice@east.test'; B='X-Actor-Email: bob@west.test'; URL=http://localhost:3000

curl -s -H "$A" "$URL/api/certificates?q=alex&sort=issued&order=desc&page=1&pageSize=25"
curl -s -H "$A" "$URL/api/certificates/1"            # issuedLocal "2026-01-11 00:30"
curl -s -H "$B" "$URL/api/certificates/8"            # issuedLocal "2026-01-10 21:30"
curl -s -H "$B" "$URL/api/certificates/1"            # 404: East certificate, West admin

curl -s -X POST -H "$A" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: demo-1' \
     -d '{"courseId": 1}' "$URL/api/bulk-issues"     # 201, 2 issued / 3 skipped
#  ... run it again: same body, header "Idempotent-Replayed: true", nothing new is written
curl -s -X POST -H "$A" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Idempotency-Key: demo-1' \
     -d '{"courseId": 2}' "$URL/api/bulk-issues"     # 409 idempotency_key_reused
curl -s -X POST -H "$B" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"courseId": 1}' "$URL/api/bulk-issues"     # 404: East course, West admin

curl -s -X POST -H "$A" "$URL/api/certificates/3/revoke"   # 200, "alreadyRevoked": false
curl -s -X POST -H "$A" "$URL/api/certificates/3/revoke"   # 200, "alreadyRevoked": true, no new audit event

curl -s -H "$A" "$URL/api/certificates/export.csv?q=lee&sort=learner&order=asc"
```

A bulk-issue response:

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "status": "completed",
  "course": { "id": 1, "title": "Safety 101" },
  "idempotencyKey": "demo-1",
  "requestedBy": "alice@east.test",
  "summary": { "total": 5, "issued": 2, "skipped": 3, "failed": 0 },
  "results": [
    { "learnerId": 1, "learnerName": "Alex Lee", "outcome": "skipped", "reason": "already_certified",
      "message": "Already certified (certificate EAST-0000001)", "certificateId": 1, "serialNumber": "EAST-0000001" },
    { "learnerId": 3, "learnerName": "Marcus O'Connor", "outcome": "issued",
      "certificateId": 12, "serialNumber": "EAST-0000008", "issuedLocal": "2026-11-23 18:33" },
    { "learnerId": 4, "learnerName": "Mei Chen", "outcome": "skipped", "reason": "not_completed",
      "message": "Course not completed (enrollment is in progress)" }
  ]
}
```

Skip reasons: `already_certified`, `not_completed`, `certificate_revoked`. A learner whose
certificate could not be written is reported as `"outcome": "failed"`; nothing is saved for that
learner, the others are unaffected, and the cause goes to the server log (not into the response):
in full for the first learner of an operation, in one line for each further one.

CSV format: UTF-8, one header row, columns `Learner Name, Course Title, Serial Number,
Issue Date (<tenant time zone>)`, dates as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm` in the tenant's time zone, RFC 4180
quoting, `\n` line endings. Cells that would be interpreted as spreadsheet formulas are neutralised.

## 6. How the acceptance criteria are met

| # | Mechanism | Verified by (`backend/test`) |
| - | --------- | ---------------------------- |
| **A1** Tenant isolation | The tenant comes only from the actor record. Every query carries `tenant_id = <actor's tenant>`; ids of other tenants behave exactly like ids that do not exist (404, same body). A cross-tenant bulk issue fails validation before anything is written. Idempotency keys are scoped to (tenant, admin), so a key can never replay another tenant's response. On top of that every reference between tenant-owned tables is a composite `(id, tenant_id)` foreign key, so cross-tenant rows cannot even be inserted. | `acceptance.test.js` › *A1 – tenant isolation* (list, detail, bulk issue, export, revoke, operations, audit; a tenant named in the query, body or headers of any endpoint; keys per admin and compared exactly); `unit.test.js` › *database layer* (each of the 13 cross-tenant references is refused by the schema) |
| **A2** Retry safety | A bulk issue is **one** `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction: look up the key → check eligibility → write certificates and audit events → store the response next to the key → commit. SQLite admits one writer at a time, so identical requests are serialised, also across processes; the first executes, all others replay the stored response byte for byte (`Idempotent-Replayed: true`). A key that has already run is answered from a plain read, without queueing for the write lock - and a request that is already queueing checks again whenever it finds the lock taken, so it gets the same answer as soon as an identical request has completed elsewhere. An operation that fails as a whole leaves nothing behind, not even its key. `UNIQUE (tenant_id, course_id, learner_id)` on certificates is the backstop. | *A2* › sequential retries, 25 concurrent requests, racing keys; **two server processes on one database** whose requests (three per server) are forced to overlap by a third connection holding the write lock; queued requests answered while the lock stays taken (the replay for the same payload, the 409 for another one); *bulk issue with injected failures* › an operation that dies after it has issued certificates |
| **A3** Key misuse | The request (method, route, canonical JSON body) is fingerprinted with SHA-256 and stored with the key. Same key + different fingerprint → `409 idempotency_key_reused`; nothing is written, and the first result stays as it was. A request whose body cannot be parsed at all (malformed, oversized, unsupported encoding) is a different request too and gets the same 409 once its key has been used. (A request that breaks off in transit is not a request yet: Node's HTTP layer answers it with a bare 400 before the application sees it, and nothing is written.) | *A3* › different course, changed payload, reordered JSON (still a replay), unreadable bodies, deeply nested JSON, concurrent misuse (also across two servers, and for a request that is already queueing for the write lock when the key gets used) |
| **A4** Learner outcomes | One classification function decides per roster row; the roster preview in the UI uses the same function. Each learner is issued inside a savepoint, so one failure becomes a `failed` outcome without undoing the others and without leaving any of that learner's rows behind. | *A4* › outcomes on Safety 101, second run, revoked certificate; *bulk issue with injected failures* › a learner failing before and after their certificate was written |
| **A5** DST & local date | Instants are stored in UTC. Local values are computed with the tenant's IANA zone through ICU (DST included). The tenant-local calendar date is stored with each certificate at issue time (`issued_local_date`) and is the leading sort key; the CSV prints the local wall-clock time. | `unit.test.js` › *time zones*; `acceptance.test.js` › *A5* (reference instant in both tenants, both 2026 DST transitions, UTC-date vs. local-date ordering, every other time shown: revocation, audit trail, roster, operation history) |
| **A6** Export at scale | See [section 7](#7-design-notes). Every ordering ends in `id`, each is backed by an index, and the export streams from a dedicated read-only connection inside a single read snapshot, in steps of 500 rows it has looked at - whether they match the filter or not - with all running exports together taking one step per event-loop iteration. | `scale.test.js` (100,000 generated rows; timings are printed), including exports whose filter matches almost nothing; `acceptance.test.js` › *export plumbing* (slots, stalled, abandoned and pipelined downloads); `unit.test.js` › *export stream*, *turn queue*, *sending a download* |
| **A7** Revocation audit | `UPDATE … WHERE status = 'active'` and the audit insert share one transaction; the audit event is written only if the update changed a row. Repeats and races return 200 with `alreadyRevoked: true` and write nothing. | *A7* › single revoke, repeats, 12 concurrent revokes; *A2 – write lock* › the same revocation sent to two servers at once (three requests each), and queued revocations overtaken by another process (certificate revoked, or gone, meanwhile) |

The UI side of these criteria - one request per click however often or wherever it is clicked,
retries that reuse the idempotency key, confirmation before revoking, truthful messages when an
answer is lost, export of exactly the current filter, loading / empty / error states - is covered
by `frontend/test`: the real application is mounted in a simulated browser and talks to a fake
server that replays answers recorded from the real backend (`frontend/test/fixtures`; refresh them
with `node frontend/test/fixtures/record.mjs` after changing the API).

Typical numbers from `npm test` on a 4-core container: filtered and sorted exports of 10,000–100,000
rows take 0.2–0.3 s each and are byte-identical across runs; while three full 100,000-row exports
stream concurrently, some 500 list requests are answered with a median of 4 ms and a worst case
under 20 ms; an export whose filter matches nothing (it still has to look at all 100,000 rows)
takes about half a second and lets some 200 list requests through meanwhile, the slowest in about
10 ms; with a download deliberately stalled mid-export, list requests and a bulk issue still
complete in milliseconds; and while the generator rewrites all 100,000 rows underneath the running
server (3–5 s), reads and replays keep being answered in under 30 ms and a bulk issue sent in the
middle completes the moment the generator commits. Measured separately with the largest allowed
`EXPORT_MAX_CONCURRENT`: with 64 full exports running at once, list requests still take 4 ms in
the median and 9 ms at the 99th percentile (2.5 ms and 6 ms on the idle server).

## 7. Design notes

**Persistence.** SQLite in WAL mode: readers never block the writer and the writer never blocks
readers. All work of a request happens on one synchronous connection, which makes each write
transaction trivially atomic; cross-process correctness comes from `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` plus database
constraints, not from the single process. The driver is `better-sqlite3`; if its native binary is
unavailable the app automatically uses Node's built-in `node:sqlite` (Node ≥ 22.13). The suite
passes on both.

**Sharing the database with other processes.** The generator, `db:reset` or a second server may
hold SQLite's write lock for a while. A request handler never sleeps inside SQLite waiting for it —
that would freeze every other request of the process. The lock is only *tried*; while it is taken
the request waits asynchronously (reads, replays and already-revoked answers are served as usual),
and after `DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 10 s) it gives up with `503` and `Retry-After`. While it
waits it keeps looking at what has been committed meanwhile: if a bulk issue with the same key
has completed on another server (the answer is its stored result, or the 409 if the payload
differs), or the certificate has been revoked by someone else, the answer is known and is given at
once, however long the lock stays taken. Several processes may also start on a brand-new database
file at the same moment: the switch to WAL mode is retried, and schema creation and seeding
re-check under the write lock, so exactly one of them does the work.

**Sorting and determinism.**

| `sort`    | ORDER BY                                                    |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `issued`  | tenant-local calendar date, then exact instant, then `id`   |
| `learner` | learner name (case and accents ignored), then `id`          |
| `course`  | course title (case and accents ignored), then `id`          |
| `serial`  | serial number, then `id`                                    |
| `status`  | status, then `id`                                           |

`id` breaks every tie, so equal sort values always come back in the same order: pages never
overlap or skip rows and two exports of the same data are identical. List and export share the
same filter/order builder, and each query is pinned to the index that stores its ordering, so a
page costs an index range scan and an export starts streaming immediately instead of sorting first.

**Search and names.** SQLite on its own treats only the 26 ASCII letters case-insensitively: a
search for `álvarez` would miss *Álvarez*, and *Élodie* would sort after *Zoe*. Every name is
therefore stored twice - as written, and folded: learners and courses carry a key column, and each
certificate carries the keys of its learner name and course title (`learner_name_key`,
`course_title_key`), computed once when the row is written. Folding unifies compatibility forms
(full-width letters, ligatures, non-breaking spaces), drops accents, lower-cases, and spells out
the Latin letters that have no accent to drop (`ø`→`o`, `ł`→`l`, `ß`→`ss`, `æ`→`ae`, `ı`→`i`, …);
other scripts are compared as written. Every ordering by name - certificate list, export, course
picker, roster and with it the order of bulk-issue results - uses the stored key; searching folds
the search text the same way and looks for it inside the key (or inside the serial number). An
accent typed on its own (`´`) is nothing to search for and matches no row; `%`, `_` and `\` in a
search are ordinary characters.

**Export without blocking.** The export opens its own read-only connection and wraps the whole
download in one read transaction: the file is a consistent snapshot even if certificates are issued
or revoked meanwhile, and the main connection stays free. SQLite calls are synchronous, so the
export must never do much in one go: it walks the tenant's rows in the requested order in steps of
500 rows it has *looked at*. The search and status filter are evaluated per row as a column of that
walk rather than in `WHERE` - otherwise "fetch the next matching row" could mean scanning the rest
of the table in a single call when few rows match. All exports of the process take their steps
through one queue, one step per event-loop iteration, so a concurrent request waits for at most one
such step (a few milliseconds) whether the filter matches everything or nothing, and however many
exports are running. Output is written with back-pressure; only the current batch is ever in memory.

Resources are bounded as well. At most `EXPORT_MAX_CONCURRENT` (4) exports read at the same time,
each on its own connection; further ones wait in arrival order without holding a connection, and
beyond 32 waiting the answer is `503 export_busy`. A client that disconnects releases its snapshot,
connection and slot within one step, even if its export has nothing to send at that moment. A
client that stays connected but takes no more data is disconnected after `EXPORT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`
(5 minutes), so a stalled download cannot pin a snapshot (and with it the write-ahead log) for
ever. "Takes no more data" is measured where the server can see it - a chunk that is ready cannot
be handed to the operating system - and the operating system buffers generously: on a fast local
connection it reports progress only about once per megabyte the client has read. A client that
reads steadily but slower than a few kB/s can therefore be cut off too; set the timeout higher, or
to `0`, for such clients. Requests that a client sends ahead on one connection without waiting for
the answers (HTTP pipelining) are answered in order, and an export among them only starts - and
only then takes a slot - when its answer can actually be sent.

**Idempotency details.** `Idempotency-Key` is optional for API callers (the UI always sends one).
Keys are 1–200 printable ASCII characters. A request that is rejected before execution (400, 404,
409, 413, 503) stores nothing, so the key is not "burned" by a typo or a busy database. Replays return the original status code
and body even if the data has changed since (for example, one of the issued certificates was
revoked later).

**Decisions worth knowing.**

- *One certificate per learner and course, ever.* A revoked certificate is not silently re-issued by
  the next bulk issue; the learner is skipped with reason `certificate_revoked`.
- *Certificates snapshot the learner name and course title.* A certificate is an issued document
  and should not change when a learner is renamed; it also keeps list, search and export join-free.
- *Audit events are per certificate* (`certificate.issued`, `certificate.revoked`), exactly one per
  issuance and one per effective revocation. A rejected or replayed request writes none.
- *No time-zone maths in the browser.* The API returns ready-to-show local strings, so UI, CSV and
  sort order cannot disagree.

**Deliberately out of scope / next steps.** Real authentication, tenant and course management,
expiring old idempotency records, re-issuing after revocation, recomputing stored local dates if a
tenant ever changed its time zone, keyset pagination and a trigram or full-text index for tenants
far beyond 10⁵ certificates (deep pages and the substring search of a *list* request are linear in
the tenant's row count today and run in one piece: tens of milliseconds at 100,000 rows), and
moving very large bulk issues to a background job.

## 9. Troubleshooting

- **Port 3000 is in use** – the server says so and exits; start it with `PORT=4000 npm start`.
- **Want a clean slate** – `npm run db:reset`. It empties and re-seeds the tables in one
  transaction, so it works while the server runs (the server simply serves the fresh data
  afterwards). If it reports that the database is busy, another process is in the middle of a
  write (for example the generator): nothing was changed, run it again in a moment.
- **"Database schema version … is not supported"** – the database file was created by a different
  version of this app. Stop the server and run `npm run db:reset`, which recreates the file.
- **A request answers `503 database_busy`** – another process held the write lock for more than

content.content:
/**
 * Text folding for search and sort.
 *
 * SQLite on its own only knows that "a" and "A" are the same letter for the 26 ASCII letters: with
 * LIKE or COLLATE NOCASE a search for "álvarez" would not find "Álvarez", and "Élodie" would sort
 * after "Zoe". Names are therefore folded once, in JavaScript, when a row is written, and the
 * folded form is stored next to the name (the `*_key` columns in the schema). Searching and
 * sorting use that stored key, and the search text goes through the same function, so both sides
 * always agree.
 *
 * The folding ignores case and accents:
 *   - compatibility forms are unified (full-width letters, ligatures, non-breaking spaces),
 *   - accents are dropped ("é" -> "e", "Å" -> "a"), and so is an accent typed on its own ("´", "¨"),
 *   - everything is lower-cased, and the two lower-case forms of the Greek sigma are unified,
 *   - the Latin letters that Unicode does not describe as "a base letter plus an accent" are
 *     replaced by the usual plain spelling ("ø" -> "o", "ł" -> "l", "ß" -> "ss", ...; see below).
 *
 * Other scripts are compared as written, apart from case: their marks are not accents and stay
 * (Devanagari vowel signs, Hangul, kana voicing marks ...).
 */

/**
 * Combining accents (U+0300-036F), together with the space that carries one when an accent stands
 * alone: NFKD turns "´" into a space plus a combining acute. Dropping only the mark would leave
 * that space behind, and a search for "´" would find every name that contains a space.
 */
const ACCENTS = / ?[\u0300-\u036f]+/g;

/** Lower-case Latin letters without a decomposition, and how they are usually written without them. */
const PLAIN_SPELLINGS = new Map([

/**
 * Text folding for search and sort.
 *
 * SQLite on its own only knows that "a" and "A" are the same letter for the 26 ASCII letters: with
 * LIKE or COLLATE NOCASE a search for "álvarez" would not find "Álvarez", and "Élodie" would sort
 * after "Zoe". Names are therefore folded once, in JavaScript, when a row is written, and the
 * folded form is stored next to the name (the `*_key` columns in the schema). Searching and
 * sorting use that stored key, and the search text goes through the same function, so both sides
 * always agree.
 *
 * The folding ignores case and accents:
 *   - compatibility forms are unified (full-width letters, ligatures, non-breaking spaces),
 *   - accents are dropped ("é" -> "e", "Å" -> "a"), and so is an accent typed on its own ("´", "¨"),
 *   - everything is lower-cased, and the two lower-case forms of the Greek sigma are unified,
 *   - the Latin letters that Unicode does not describe as "a base letter plus an accent" are
 *     replaced by the usual plain spelling ("ø" -> "o", "ł" -> "l", "ß" -> "ss", ...; see below).
 *
 * Other scripts are compared as written, apart from case: their marks are not accents and stay
 * (Devanagari vowel signs, Hangul, kana voicing marks ...).
 */

/**
 * Combining accents (U+0300-036F), together with the space that carries one when an accent stands
 * alone: NFKD turns "´" into a space plus a combining acute. Dropping only the mark would leave
 * that space behind, and a search for "´" would find every name that contains a space.
 */
const ACCENTS = / ?[\u0300-\u036f]+/g;

/** Lower-case Latin letters without a decomposition, and how they are usually written without them. */
const PLAIN_SPELLINGS = new Map([
  ['ß', 'ss'],
  ['æ', 'ae'],
  ['œ', 'oe'],
  ['ø', 'o'],
  ['đ', 'd'],
  ['ð', 'd'],
  ['þ', 'th'],
  ['ł', 'l'],
  ['ħ', 'h'],
  ['ŧ', 't'],
  ['ı', 'i'], // Turkish dotless i ("İ" already folds to "i" through its decomposition)
]);
const LETTERS_WITH_PLAIN_SPELLING = new RegExp(`[${[...PLAIN_SPELLINGS.keys()].join('')}]`, 'g');

export function foldText(text) {
  return String(text)
    .normalize('NFKD')
    .replace(ACCENTS, '')
    .toLowerCase()
    .replaceAll('ς', 'σ')
    .replace(LETTERS_WITH_PLAIN_SPELLING, (letter) => PLAIN_SPELLINGS.get(letter))
    .normalize('NFC');
}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Mutation check, round 3: the round-2 mutants adapted to the current code, plus mutants for the round-3 changes.

usage: mutate3.py [--work DIR] [--list] [--check] [--new] [name ...]
  --check  only verify that every mutant still applies to the current sources (no tests are run)
  --new    run only the mutants added or changed in round 3
"""
import os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import mutate2 as base

SRC = base.SRC
ROOT = base.ROOT
U, A, S = base.U, base.A, base.S
M = dict(base.MUTANTS)

T_QUEUED_BULK = 'queued bulk issues are answered once a request with their key has completed elsewhere, however long the lock stays taken'
T_QUEUED_GONE = 'a queued revocation is answered once the certificate has disappeared, however long the lock stays taken'
T_MANY_FAIL = 'when many learners of one operation fail, the cause is logged in full once and in one line for each of the others'
T_PIPE = 'requests sent ahead on one connection (pipelining) hold no slot until they can be answered, and nothing once the connection is gone'
T_PIPE_IDLE = 'a pipelining client that never reads is dropped after the idle timeout, with everything it held'
T_PIPE_READ = 'pipelined requests that are read get their answers one after the other, each complete'
T_ABANDONED_HTTP = 'an export nobody is waiting for any more stops reading, even when it has nothing to send'
T_ABANDONED_UNIT = 'an abandoned export stops before its next step instead of reading to the end'
T_HEAD = 'HEAD announces the download without running it'
T_ONE_STEP = 'takes steps of 500 rows, and all exports together take one step per event-loop iteration'
T_TURNS = 'lets exactly one step through per event-loop iteration, first come first served'
T_SEND_STALL = 'gives up on a destination that takes nothing more for the idle timeout'
T_SEND_SLOW = 'leaves a slow destination alone as long as it keeps taking data'
T_SEND_SOURCE = 'does not count the time the source needs'
T_SEND_TAIL = 'applies the timeout to the buffered tail as well, after the source has finished'
T_SEND_SIGNAL = 'waits as long as it takes when the timeout is 0, until the signal ends the transfer'
T_LONE_ACCENT = 'drops an accent typed on its own instead of turning it into a space'
T_PLAIN_UNIT = 'spells out the Latin letters that have no accent to drop'
T_PLAIN_HTTP = 'finds and sorts the Latin letters that have no accent to drop (ø, ł, ß, ı ...) by their plain spelling'
T_COURSE_SORT = 'sorts course titles the same way - in the certificate list, the export and the course picker'
T_ROSTER = 'lists a course roster - and with it the outcomes of a bulk issue - by name, ignoring case and accents'
T_KEYS = 'stores every name together with its folded form, which is what gets sorted and searched'
T_ALIASES = 'refuses two names of the same parameter instead of ignoring one of them'
T_CASE = 'reads status, sort and order in any letter case'
T_LENGTH = 'counts the length of the search text in characters, not in UTF-16 units'
T_PATTERNS = 'treats %, _ and other pattern characters in the search text literally'
T_PORT = 'a port that is already taken is reported in one line, not as a crash'
T_SLOTS = base.T_SLOTS
T_IDLE = base.T_IDLE
T_ENV = base.T_ENV_SLOTS
T_CLI = base.T_CLI
T_SETTINGS = base.T_SETTINGS
T_GENERATOR = base.T_GENERATOR
T_ACCENTS = base.T_ACCENTS
T_FAIL_BEFORE = base.T_FAIL_BEFORE
T_UNIT_SETTINGS = 'rejects unusable values in one line each'

NEW = set()

def put(name, **spec):
    M[name] = spec
    NEW.add(name)

def retarget(name, **changes):
    M[name] = {**M[name], **changes}
    NEW.add(name)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- round-2 mutants whose code moved or changed
for name in ('no-while-waiting-bulk', 'while-waiting-ignored'):
    retarget(name, expect=[T_QUEUED_BULK if t == base.T_QUEUED_BULK else t for t in M[name]['expect']])
retarget('blank-not-absent', old="    if (text === '') continue;\n", new="")
retarget('integer-nine-digits', old="  if (!/^\\d+$/.test(given.text))", new="  if (!/^\\d{1,9}$/.test(given.text))")
retarget('export-reader-never-closed', file='src/services/certificates.js', old="      reader.close();\n", new="",
         tests=[U, A], expect=['looks at a fixed number of rows per step, whether they match or not', base.T_CLOSED])
retarget('export-no-idle-timeout', file='src/lib/download.js', old="      if (over || idleTimeoutMs <= 0) return;\n", new="      return;\n",
         tests=[U, A, S], expect=[T_SEND_STALL, T_SEND_TAIL, T_IDLE, T_PIPE_IDLE, T_ENV])
retarget('export-idle-timer-keeps-running', file='src/lib/download.js',
         old="          yield chunk; // resumes when the stream asks for more, i.e. the destination made room\n          clearTimeout(idleTimer);\n",
         new="          yield chunk; // resumes when the stream asks for more, i.e. the destination made room\n",
         tests=[U, A], expect=[T_SEND_SLOW, T_IDLE])
retarget('export-slot-never-released', old="      release?.();\n", new="", expect=[T_SLOTS])
retarget('export-slot-kept-after-failed-start',
         edits=[("      release?.();\n", ""), ("      if (outcome.stalled) {", "      release();\n      if (outcome.stalled) {")],

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Mutation check, round 2: put one defect into a throw-away copy of the backend and run the tests that should catch it.

usage: mutate2.py [--work DIR] [--list] [name ...]
"""
import os, re, shutil, subprocess, sys

SRC = '/home/user/cert-admin-console/backend'
ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

U = 'test/unit.test.js'
A = 'test/acceptance.test.js'
S = 'test/scale.test.js'

RECURSIVE = '''export function canonicalJson(value) {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return `[${value.map(canonicalJson).join(',')}]`;
  if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') {
    return `{${Object.keys(value).filter((key) => value[key] !== undefined).sort().map((key) => `${JSON.stringify(key)}:${canonicalJson(value[key])}`).join(',')}}`;
  }
  return JSON.stringify(value) ?? 'null';
}

/**
 * Stable hash'''

T_FK = "refuses references to another tenant's enrollment, bulk operation or certificate"
T_OVERLAP = 'identical requests to two servers overlap for certain and still execute exactly once'
T_STORED = 'a key that already ran needs no lock: replays, conflicts and rejections are answered at once'
T_REVOKE_LOCK = 'a new revocation waits for the lock, then takes effect once'
T_QUEUED_BULK = 'a queued bulk issue is answered once an identical request has completed elsewhere, however long the lock stays taken'
T_QUEUED_REVOKE = 'a queued revocation is answered once somebody else has revoked the certificate, however long the lock stays taken'
T_ATOMIC = 'an operation that fails as a whole leaves nothing behind - not even its idempotency key'
T_FAIL_BEFORE = 'a learner who fails before anything is written is reported as failed; the others are issued'
T_FAIL_AFTER = 'a learner who fails after their certificate was written leaves no partial writes'
T_ACCENTS = 'finds accented names however they are typed: case and accents do not count'
T_SORT_NAMES = 'sorts names ignoring case and accents, and finds special characters as themselves'
T_ONLY_NAMES = 'searches learner names and serial numbers only'
T_UNIT_REJECT = 'rejects values it does not understand'
T_BAD_PARAMS = 'rejects malformed list parameters with a 400'
T_UNIT_BLANK = 'treats a blank parameter as not given'
T_BLANK = 'a blank parameter counts as not given, and no parameter is ever dropped silently'
T_AUDIT = 'audit events: filters are validated like everything else'
T_PAGES = 'counts pages correctly, also when the total is an exact multiple of the page size'
T_PLAN = 'keeps the filter out of WHERE, so that no single step depends on how many rows match'
T_STEP = 'looks at a fixed number of rows per step, whether they match or not'
T_SELECTIVE = 'an export whose filter matches next to nothing does not hold other requests up either'
T_RESPONSIVE = 'list requests stay responsive while exports are streaming at full speed'
T_SAME_AS_LIST = 'exports exactly what the list shows for the same search and sort'
T_CLOSED = 'every export closes its connection: after a complete download and after an abandoned one'
T_IDLE = 'a download whose client stops reading is dropped after the idle timeout; one that keeps reading is not'
T_SLOTS = 'only so many exports read at a time: the others wait their turn, and a full queue answers 503'
T_ENV_SLOTS = T_ENV_IDLE = 'EXPORT_MAX_CONCURRENT and EXPORT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS: an export waits for the only slot until the stalled download holding it is dropped'
T_TENANT_CLAIM = 'naming another tenant in the query, the body or a header changes nothing, on any endpoint'
T_KEY_SCOPE = 'idempotency keys belong to one admin - also within a tenant - and are compared exactly'
T_TIMES = 'shows every other time in the tenant zone as well: revocation, audit trail, roster, bulk-issue results'
T_GENERATOR = 'the load-test generator leaves every quick-start row alone - serial counters included - and repeats itself exactly'
T_SETTINGS = 'every setting is checked before anything starts, each with its own one-line message'
T_CLI = 'the command-line scripts report mistakes briefly, without a stack trace, and change nothing'
T_WAL_REAL = 'opening a new file while another process writes to it waits for the WAL switch instead of failing'
T_WAL_STANDIN = 'retries the switch to WAL journaling while simultaneous openers make SQLite report busy'
def apply(name, root):
    m = M[name]
    path = os.path.join(root, m['file'])
    text = open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()
    for old, new in edits_of(m, text):
        assert text.count(old) == 1, f"{name}: pattern occurs {text.count(old)} times in {m['file']}: {old[:70]!r}"
        text = text.replace(old, new)
    return path, text

FROZEN = None  # a copy of the sources taken once per invocation: the live tree may change while a batch runs

def freeze(work):
    global FROZEN
    FROZEN = os.path.join(work, '_frozen-backend')
    shutil.rmtree(FROZEN, ignore_errors=True)
    os.makedirs(work, exist_ok=True)
    shutil.copytree(SRC, FROZEN, ignore=shutil.ignore_patterns('node_modules'))

def run(name, work):
    m = M[name]
    shutil.rmtree(os.path.join(work, 'backend'), ignore_errors=True)
    os.makedirs(work, exist_ok=True)
    shutil.copytree(FROZEN, os.path.join(work, 'backend'))
    if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(work, 'node_modules')):
        os.symlink('/home/user/cert-admin-console/node_modules', os.path.join(work, 'node_modules'))
    path, text = apply(name, os.path.join(work, 'backend'))
    open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(text)
    env = dict(os.environ, DB_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS='3000')
    cmd = ['node', '--test', '--test-reporter=tap', '--test-concurrency=1', '--test-timeout=120000'] + m['tests']
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=os.path.join(work, 'backend'), env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=420)
        out = proc.stdout
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as e:
        out = (e.stdout or b'').decode() if isinstance(e.stdout, bytes) else (e.stdout or '')
        out += '\n not ok 0 - (the test run did not finish within 420 s)\n'
        subprocess.run(['pkill', '-f', os.path.join(work, 'backend')], capture_output=True)
    failed = sorted(set(re.findall(r'^\s*not ok \d+ - (.+)$', out, re.M)))
    failed = [t for t in failed if not t.startswith(SUITES) or t in m['expect']]
    failed = [t for t in failed if not t.startswith('test/')]
    missing = [t for t in m['expect'] if t not in failed]
    verdict = 'KILLED' if failed and not missing else ('SURVIVED' if not failed else 'PARTIAL')
    if m.get('equivalent') and not failed:
        verdict = 'EQUIVALENT'
    if verdict != 'KILLED' and 'test timed out' in out:
        verdict = 'KILLED-BY-HANG'  # a test never finished and the run was stopped by --test-timeout
    print(f"{verdict:9} {name}: {len(failed)} failing")
    for t in failed:
        marker = '*' if t in m['expect'] else ' '
        print(f"      {marker} {t}")
    for t in missing:
        print(f"      ! expected to fail but passed: {t}")
    sys.stdout.flush()

if __name__ == '__main__':

    cmd = ['node', '--test', '--test-reporter=tap', '--test-concurrency=1', '--test-timeout=1800000'] + m['tests']

const COMMON = `You are one of five independent verifiers of a small software project just before it is handed over. The author believes everything works. Your job is to prove otherwise in your area - or to establish, with evidence you produced yourself, that it holds. Be adversarial but honest: report only what you reproduced; do not pad the report with speculation.

THE PROJECT
"Multi-Tenant Certificate Admin Console": an internal admin console where tenant admins review course completions, bulk-issue certificates, revoke them and export them as CSV. Backend: Node.js (ESM), Express 5, SQLite in WAL mode (driver better-sqlite3, automatic fallback to the built-in node:sqlite). Frontend: React 19 + Vite. No login: every API request names its actor in the header X-Actor-Email (alice@east.test -> tenant East, Australia/Sydney; bob@west.test -> tenant West, Australia/Perth). One documented command starts everything: "npm start" (installs, builds the UI, creates the demo database, serves UI + API on one port). "npm test" runs the verification suites (API tests with node:test, then UI tests with Vitest).
- The original task specification: ${S}/final/SPEC.md  (read it first; acceptance criteria A1-A7 are at the end)
- The project as it will be handed over (frozen, READ-ONLY, 72 files): ${S}/final/app   (manifest: ${S}/final/manifest.sha256). Its README.md describes behaviour, API, settings and design; treat every statement in it as a claim to check, not as truth.
- What the backend changed in the last round, as a diff: ${S}/final/backend-round3.diff

GROUND RULES
1. Work only inside your own directory ${S}/final/<your-area>/ (create it). Make your private copy first:  cp -r ${S}/final/app ${S}/final/<your-area>/app && chmod -R u+w ${S}/final/<your-area>/app , then run "npm ci --no-audit --no-fund" in it (seconds; the npm cache is warm). Never write to ${S}/final/app, to /home/user/cert-admin-console, or to another verifier's directory.
2. Ports: use only the port range given to you below. Start servers with PORT=<port> HOST=127.0.0.1 and with DB_PATH=<a file inside your directory> (or --db for the CLI scripts). Never use the default port 3000. "npm test" needs no settings: it uses ephemeral ports and temp directories.
3. Record the PID of every long-running process you start (server, vite, helper scripts) and stop each one by PID before you finish; check that your ports no longer answer. If stopping a process is refused, say so in your summary with PID and port.
4. Node versions on this machine: default "node" is 22.23.5 (npm 10.9.9); Node 20.20.2 (npm 10.8.2) is at ${S}/node20/node-v20.20.2-linux-x64/bin; Node 24.22.3 (npm 11.19.1) is at /opt/node24/bin - put the directory first in PATH to use one. A native module installed under one Node version does not load under another: use a separate copy (and npm ci) per Node version. Chromium and Playwright are pre-installed: require('playwright') works from any directory, chromium.launch() needs no options; do not install browsers. python3 is available (sqlite3, unicodedata, zoneinfo) for independent oracles.
5. The machine has 4 cores and other verifiers and test runs are active at the same time. Treat a single slow measurement with suspicion: repeat it, and say when load may explain a number. Do not report a timing finding you could not repeat.
6. A finding needs a reproduction you ran yourself: exact commands or steps, what you observed, what you expected. Severity: critical = wrong or lost data, or an acceptance criterion violated; major = a spec requirement or documented feature fails in a realistic situation; minor = wrong in an edge case, misleading message or documentation, or an important behaviour without any test; nit = cosmetic or very unlikely. Things the README lists as deliberately out of scope are not findings, and neither is the absence of real authentication (the spec forbids adding it).
7. When you are done, return your result through the structured output: a summary, what you checked (with numbers), and the findings (an empty list if you found nothing wrong).

`

+A download that cannot be completed never ends quietly. When the server gives one up (the idle
+timeout, a failure while reading) it resets the connection instead of closing it, so that a client
+which does not check how the body is framed - HTTP/1.0, a simple script - cannot take half a file
+for a whole one. The other side of that rule: a client has to keep its sending side open until the
+download is complete. One that half-closes the connection right after its request (`nc -N`, a
+`shutdown(SHUT_WR)` in a script) cannot be told from one that has left, and gets the reset too.
+Browsers, `curl`, `wget` and HTTP libraries do not do that.

+- **"…was installed with another Node.js version"** – the native SQLite module is built for one
+  Node.js version. After switching versions run `npm rebuild better-sqlite3` (the message says so),
+  or start with `SQLITE_DRIVER=node` on Node ≥ 22.13.
+- **"the database cannot be written to"** – the database file or its directory is read-only for
+  the user running the server. The server needs to write there (also for reads: SQLite keeps its
+  write-ahead log next to the file); fix the permissions or point `DB_PATH` somewhere else.
+- **`npm run dev` says the dependencies are not installed** – it does not install anything itself:
+  run `npm start` (or `npm install`) once first.

const missing = AREAS.filter((_, index) => !results[index]).map((area) => area.key)

const digest = completed

    const findings = result.findings.map((finding) => '    - [' + finding.severity + '] ' + finding.title).join('\n') || '    (none)'
    const checks = result.checksPerformed.map((check) => '    - ' + check).join('\n')
    return '== ' + result.area + ' ==\n  summary: ' + result.summary + '\n  checks performed:\n' + checks + '\n  findings:\n' + findings
  })

- 批量签发：结果“可能已执行”或“尚未执行”时，课程选择会锁定，直到点“安全重试”或“忽略”，重试提示和幂等键不会再因切换课程而丢失。
- 批量签发：完成后会在状态区显示并播报结果摘要。
- 详情抽屉和撤销确认框：Tab 焦点不再跑到后面的页面，请求进行中的确认框也无法从键盘绕过关闭。
- 顶栏不再遮挡获得焦点的控件；小窗口下顶栏随页面滚动。
- 多行撤销原因按原样换行显示。
- 回归时在 Node 20 上发现下载读取失败时错误原因被报成“提前关闭”，导致两条单元测试失败，已修复。

**已验证的结果**
- `npm test` 在 Node 20、22、24 的全新副本上都通过：接口 190 项、界面 252 项，无跳过，约 1 分钟。
- Node 22 上还在内置 SQLite 驱动、`NODE_ENV=production` 加一组故意设错的环境变量下各跑了一遍，均通过。
- 真实浏览器里重跑了上一轮验证留下的 33 份脚本（约 3,300 项检查），剩下的不一致都是预期中的行为变化，例如状态区现在有结果摘要、课程选择被锁定。
- 本轮新增和改动的 36 个后端变异用例中，32 个被测试抓住，其余 4 个是等价变异。
- 全新副本上的 `npm start`（含删除 lockfile 的情况）、生成 10 万条数据、重置、开发模式都能正常运行。

**其他改动**
- “只读数据库在启动时被拒绝”这条测试原来在 root 下会被跳过，现在改为以 `nobody` 身份启动服务器，在容器里也能真正执行。
- README 已同步更新：测试数量、设置项、搜索与导出的说明、故障排查条目，以及实测内存（空闲约 65 MB，64 个并发导出约 330 MB）。
- 快照冻结之后我又改了一处 `scripts/dev.mjs`，让开发模式在指定 `HOST` 时也能连上接口。这处改动只做了手动验证，不在本轮独立验证的范围内。

中途我发现这台机器没有 `ss` 命令，之前几次按端口结束进程实际没有生效，留下了 6 个自己起的测试服务器，现已逐个关闭。

summary: I tested the frontend in Chromium through Playwright against the real backend, on both builds: the production build (npm start, port 7050) and the Vite dev server in StrictMode (port 7053, API on 7052). For the 100,000-row and layout checks I used a second backend on 7055 with a generated database, plus a second Vite server on 7056.

Nine of the ten previous findings are gone on both builds.
- Bulk issue lock: I ran 49 timing variants per build, each starting with one real click. Over 98 rounds there was never a second POST or a second operation. The button comes back once the reloaded roster arrives, as 'Issue 1 certificate' when a learner failed, and also after a failed roster reload followed by Try again.
- Retry prompt: the course picker is locked and the prompt keeps its key through every disruption I tried (all listed in the checks). After db:reset, Retry starts a fresh operation. If the course is deleted, Retry reports 'was rejected – Course not found' and Dismiss frees the picker.
- Announcements: the live region exists before its text changes. The start, success, partial failure and replay texts are announced. Nothing is announced on a plain load, a reload or a return to the tab. 'Show outcomes' focuses the result heading.
- Modal dialogs: Tab and Shift+Tab never leave the top dialog. Nothing behind is focusable (inert), and Chrome's own accessibility tree contains only the dialog. Playwright's ariaSnapshot still lists the page behind because it ignores 'inert'; that is a tool limit, not an app bug. A confirmation whose request is in flight survives every key sequence and click I tried. Every way of closing leaves no inert attribute behind and focus goes back where it came from.
- Top bar: nothing focused or scrolled to ends up hidden at any of the six window sizes, including 100 rows over 100,007 certificates. The README is right that the bar sticks on large windows and scrolls away below 720 px wide or 480 px high, also when the window is resized.
- Smaller fixes hold: revocation reasons keep their line breaks and long words wrap at 360 px; exports that are not CSV are refused and real ones match curl byte for byte (also 7.5 MB, all East rows); switching the actor sends no request for the previous tenant's id.

What still fails:
1. A double click on a learner name in the list still opens the drawer and selects nothing. The first click of a double click is a plain click, so the new selection check never sees a selection. Dragging and shift-click are fixed. The previous finding named double click explicitly and the task asks for it, so that finding is only partly fixed.
2. The README says a confirmation whose request is on its way 'can neither be closed nor bypassed'. The browser's Back button (or Alt+Left) closes both drawer and confirmation mid-request. The revocation still completes and the list then shows Revoked, so no data is lost, but the README claim does not hold for browser navigation.

Regressions: none found. The four workflo

content.content:
NEW RESULT: backend-adversarial
The backend mostly holds up. I found two new problems: one minor and one nit.

What holds, with evidence I produced myself:
- Exports. On Node 22, 20 and 24, the server sends a real reset whenever it gives a download up: idle timeout, a read failure (database corrupted mid-export, both drivers), or a client that half-closes. strace shows SO_LINGER 0 and then close, with no shutdown call.
- Ordinary clients all got byte-identical full 100,000-row files (sha256 1541ef71...): curl, curl --http1.0, wget, urllib, http.client (twice on one connection), node fetch (twice) and a Playwright browser download (twice).
- No client that did nothing wrong was ever reset. This covers pipelined requests (export first, export last, 3 and 10 exports), a request sent in two packets 3.5 s apart, a 1.5 s stall, and a steady reader at about 160 kB/s against the default timeout.
- After the abuse runs, export slots were free, the server's sqlite file descriptors stayed constant (4 after 30 further exports), wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) from python returned (0,0,0), and the server logs held only "download dropped" lines (plus the expected stack trace from the deliberate corruption test).
- Memory (RSS): about 84 MB idle, 94 MB with 1 export, 116 MB with 4, 144 MB with 16, 283 MB peak with 64 (359 MB kept afterwards). This is close to the README's numbers. List latency stayed bounded (median 11-15 ms for a heavy search query), but the load average was 9.4 on 4 cores, so I make no timing claim.
- Read-only databases, run as user nobody with both drivers: each case ended in one line, exit 1, within 0.1-0.5 s, and the database file's bytes were unchanged. A writable file with writable -wal/-shm in a read-only directory starts and accepts writes, which is correct. A database another process is writing to starts promptly, and starting leaves its bytes unchanged.
- Settings: 31 values checked. Blank or white-space values count as not set. LOG_REQUESTS accepts 0 and 1 only. Every bad value is reported in one line before the port is taken, and no database file is created. The start-up line names the right address.
- Command-line scripts through npm: --db is handed on. A reset shrinks the file to fresh size (167,936 bytes, no sqlite_stat tables), also while a server or an idle reader has it open.
- Search: accents and spaces alone match nothing. The python oracle agreed on 48 queries, apart from the documented ø/ł/æ/œ/ð/þ spellings. All the alias and direction conflicts answer 400. List, total, pages and export agreed on 9 filters.
- Core: 30 concurrent identical bulk issues split over two servers (one per driver) ran as one operation. Every key reuse got 409. A 20-way revocation race wrote one audit event. Tenant isolation held. integrity_check and foreign_key_check were clean.

What does not hold:
1. Minor: a failed start on a read-only database leaves -wal/-shm files behind (the -shm read-only), so the README's fix ("fix the permissions") does not work afterwards.
2. Nit: the reset only protects clients whose network stack reports it. OpenBSD nc (named in the README) and Node/libuv sockets treat it as a clean end, so `nc -N` gets "200 OK" plus only the CSV header and exits 0.

Things the integrator must know:
- Rule breaches:

====================================================================================================
--- title: A failed start on a read-only database leaves a read-only -shm behind, so the start stays refused after the permission is fixed
--- severity: minor
--- category: robustness
--- description: When the database file is read-only (no -wal/-shm present), the refused start still creates db.sqlite-shm (32 KB) and db.sqlite-wal (0 bytes), owned by the user who tried. SQLite gives them the database file's mode, so both are r--r--r--. If the owner then does what the README troubleshooting entry says ('fix the permissions', chmod 644 db.sqlite) and starts again, the start is refused with the same message 'the database cannot be written to (attempt to write a readonly database)'. The cause is now the leftover read-only -shm that the server created, not the database file. In a shared directory the leftovers belong to whoever tried, so another user is blocked as well. This also contradicts 'a failed start leaves nothing behind' (README: a start that fails on a setting or on the port does not leave a database file behind). It happens with both drivers.
--- reproduction: As root: N=/tmp/x; mkdir -m 777 $N/chain. As nobody (runuser -u nobody -- env HOME=.. TMPDIR=..): node scripts/init-db.js --db $N/chain/db.sqlite; chmod 444 $N/chain/db.sqlite; PORT=7110 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=$N/chain/db.sqlite node src/server.js -> 'Could not open the database at ...: the database cannot be written to (attempt to write a readonly database)', exit 1. ls -la now shows db.sqlite-shm -r--r--r-- nobody 32768 and db.sqlite-wal -r--r--r-- nobody 0, which did not exist before. Then chmod 644 db.sqlite and start again -> the same one-line refusal, exit 1. The same leftovers appear when the read-only file belongs to root (the -shm then belongs to nobody, mode 444), and with SQLITE_DRIVER=node.
--- expected: A refused start leaves the directory as it found it. After the database file's permission is fixed, the next start works, or the message names the file that is actually in the way.
--- reproduced: True
--- location: backend/src/db/sqlite.js openDatabase/enableWal + Connection.assertWritable; backend/src/bootstrap.js
--- suggestedFix: Before opening, check fs.accessSync(file, W_OK) for an existing database (and its existing -wal/-shm). Or, when assertWritable fails, close the connection and remove any -wal/-shm that did not exist before the attempt. Mention leftover -shm/-wal in the troubleshooting entry.
====================================================================================================
--- title: The connection reset does not reach every client: OpenBSD nc and Node/libuv sockets take a truncated export for a complete one
--- severity: nit
--- category: docs
--- description: README section 7 says the server resets a download it gives up 'so that a client which does not check how the body is framed - HTTP/1.0, a simple script - cannot take half a file for a whole one', and that `nc -N` 'gets the reset too'. The server does send the reset (strace: SO_LINGER 0, then close). But OpenBSD netcat, the nc the README names, sees POLLERR|POLLHUP and exits 0 without an error message, so the half file is silently taken as complete. Node.js raw sockets do the same: libuv reports a short read followed by POLLHUP as a normal end, so 'end' fires without an error. For nc -N this is exactly the previous round's symptom: a filtered export arrives as '200 OK' plus only the CSV header, which looks like 'no certificates match'. The behaviour is the client's, but the README promises protection that does not reach the tool it names.
--- reproduction: Server: EXPORT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=3000, 100k database, port 7100.
(1) printf 'GET /api/certificates/export.csv?q=EAST-LT-000001 HTTP/1.0\r\nX-Actor-Email: alice@east.test\r\n\r\n' | nc -N 127.0.0.1 7100 > out; echo $? -> 0. out has 9 lines: the status line and headers, then only the CSV header. curl for the same URL gives 11 lines (header + 10 rows).
(2) (printf 'GET /api/certificates/export.csv HTTP/1.0\r\n...\r\n\r\n'; sleep 12) | nc 127.0.0.1 7100 | (sleep 6; cat > out) -> exit 0, 70,933 bytes, no message; strace of nc shows poll -> POLLERR|POLLHUP then exit_group(0). The same pipeline with curl --http1.0 exits 56.
(3) A Node net client (HTTP/1.0) that pauses for 6 s: 'end' event, no 'error', 165-783 KB of 7.5 MB, 5 of 5 runs on servers under Node 20, 22 and 24. Python sockets see ConnectionResetError in the same situations.
--- expected: Either the README says that some clients (nc, Node raw sockets) treat the reset as a normal end and keep the half file, or such clients get the whole file.
--- reproduced: True
--- location: README.md section 7 ('A download that cannot be completed never ends quietly ...'); backend/src/app.js export route
--- suggestedFix: Change the README so it no longer promises this for nc: name the clients that report the reset (curl, wget, browsers, Python) and say nc and raw Node sockets do not. For the half-close case, the server could keep sending after the client's FIN (for example Node's server.httpAllowHalfOpen = true, without the reset on 'end'). That would give nc -N the complete file; it is a suggestion I did not test.

--- title: A failed start on a read-only database leaves a read-only -shm behind, so the start stays refused after the permission is fixed
--- severity: minor
--- category: robustness
--- description: When the database file is read-only (no -wal/-shm present), the refused start still creates db.sqlite-shm (32 KB) and db.sqlite-wal (0 bytes), owned by the user who tried. SQLite gives them the database file's mode, so both are r--r--r--. If the owner then does what the README troubleshooting entry says ('fix the permissions', chmod 644 db.sqlite) and starts again, the start is refused with the same message 'the database cannot be written to (attempt to write a readonly database)'. The cause is now the leftover read-only -shm that the server created, not the database file. In a shared directory the leftovers belong to whoever tried, so another user is blocked as well. This also contradicts 'a failed start leaves nothing behind' (README: a start that fails on a setting or on the port does not leave a database file behind). It happens with both drivers.
--- reproduction: As root: N=/tmp/x; mkdir -m 777 $N/chain. As nobody (runuser -u nobody -- env HOME=.. TMPDIR=..): node scripts/init-db.js --db $N/chain/db.sqlite; chmod 444 $N/chain/db.sqlite; PORT=7110 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=$N/chain/db.sqlite node src/server.js -> 'Could not open the database at ...: the database cannot be written to (attempt to write a readonly database)', exit 1. ls -la now shows db.sqlite-shm -r--r--r-- nobody 32768 and db.sqlite-wal -r--r--r-- nobody 0, which did not exist before. Then chmod 644 db.sqlite and start again -> the same one-line refusal, exit 1. The same leftovers appear when the read-only file belongs to root (the -shm then belongs to nobody, mode 444), and with SQLITE_DRIVER=node.
--- expected: A refused start leaves the directory as it found it. After the database file's permission is fixed, the next start works, or the message names the file that is actually in the way.
--- reproduced: True
--- location: backend/src/db/sqlite.js openDatabase/enableWal + Connection.assertWritable; backend/src/bootstrap.js
--- suggestedFix: Before opening, check fs.accessSync(file, W_OK) for an existing database (and its existing -wal/-shm). Or, when assertWritable fails, close the connection and remove any -wal/-shm that did not exist before the attempt. Mention leftover -shm/-wal in the troubleshooting entry.

--- title: The connection reset does not reach every client: OpenBSD nc and Node/libuv sockets take a truncated export for a complete one
--- severity: nit
--- category: docs
--- description: README section 7 says the server resets a download it gives up 'so that a client which does not check how the body is framed - HTTP/1.0, a simple script - cannot take half a file for a whole one', and that `nc -N` 'gets the reset too'. The server does send the reset (strace: SO_LINGER 0, then close). But OpenBSD netcat, the nc the README names, sees POLLERR|POLLHUP and exits 0 without an error message, so the half file is silently taken as complete. Node.js raw sockets do the same: libuv reports a short read followed by POLLHUP as a normal end, so 'end' fires without an error. For nc -N this is exactly the previous round's symptom: a filtered export arrives as '200 OK' plus only the CSV header, which looks like 'no certificates match'. The behaviour is the client's, but the README promises protection that does not reach the tool it names.
--- reproduction: Server: EXPORT_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=3000, 100k database, port 7100.
(1) printf 'GET /api/certificates/export.csv?q=EAST-LT-000001 HTTP/1.0\r\nX-Actor-Email: alice@east.test\r\n\r\n' | nc -N 127.0.0.1 7100 > out; echo $? -> 0. out has 9 lines: the status line and headers, then only the CSV header. curl for the same URL gives 11 lines (header + 10 rows).
(2) (printf 'GET /api/certificates/export.csv HTTP/1.0\r\n...\r\n\r\n'; sleep 12) | nc 127.0.0.1 7100 | (sleep 6; cat > out) -> exit 0, 70,933 bytes, no message; strace of nc shows poll -> POLLERR|POLLHUP then exit_group(0). The same pipeline with curl --http1.0 exits 56.
(3) A Node net client (HTTP/1.0) that pauses for 6 s: 'end' event, no 'error', 165-783 KB of 7.5 MB, 5 of 5 runs on servers under Node 20, 22 and 24. Python sockets see ConnectionResetError in the same situations.
--- expected: Either the README says that some clients (nc, Node raw sockets) treat the reset as a normal end and keep the half file, or such clients get the whole file.
--- reproduced: True
--- location: README.md section 7 ('A download that cannot be completed never ends quietly ...'); backend/src/app.js export route
--- suggestedFix: Change the README so it no longer promises this for nc: name the clients that report the reset (curl, wget, browsers, Python) and say nc and raw Node sockets do not. For the half-close case, the server could keep sending after the client's FIN (for example Node's server.httpAllowHalfOpen = true, without the reset on 'end'). That would give nc -N the complete file; it is a suggestion I did not test.

is left exactly as it was found. The line printed after a successful start names the address to
open: `localhost` when the server listens on all interfaces, the configured `HOST` otherwise.
""")

rep("""A download that cannot be completed never ends quietly. When the server gives one up (the idle
timeout, a failure while reading) it resets the connection instead of closing it, so that a client
which does not check how the body is framed - HTTP/1.0, a simple script - cannot take half a file
for a whole one. The other side of that rule: a client has to keep its sending side open until the
download is complete. One that half-closes the connection right after its request (`nc -N`, a
`shutdown(SHUT_WR)` in a script) cannot be told from one that has left, and gets the reset too.
Browsers, `curl`, `wget` and HTTP libraries do not do that.
""", """A download that cannot be completed never ends quietly. When the server gives one up (the idle
timeout, a failure while reading) it resets the connection instead of closing it. An HTTP/1.1
client sees from the framing of the body that the file is incomplete either way; the reset is for
the clients that have no framing to go by - HTTP/1.0, a simple script - and helps as far as their
network code passes it on: `curl --http1.0` and Python sockets report it as an error, whereas
netcat and raw Node.js sockets treat a reset that follows data as a plain end and keep the part
they received.

The other side of that rule: a client has to keep its sending side open until the download is
complete. One that half-closes the connection right after its request (`nc -N`, a
`shutdown(SHUT_WR)` in a script) cannot be told from one that has left - and an export must not
keep reading for a client that is gone, least of all one that has nothing to send to it at the
moment - so its download is cut short, with the same reset. Browsers, `curl`, `wget` and HTTP
libraries do not half-close.
""")

rep("""- **"the database cannot be written to" / "attempt to write a readonly database"** – the database
  file or its directory is read-only for the user running the server. The server needs to write
  to both (SQLite keeps its write-ahead log next to the file); fix the permissions or point
  `DB_PATH` somewhere else.
""", """- **"the database cannot be written to (…)"** – the user running the server may not write the
  database file, a `-wal` / `-shm` file next to it, or (when those two do not exist yet) the
  directory; the text in brackets says which. The server needs all of them: SQLite keeps its
  write-ahead log next to the database. Fix the permissions - a read-only `-wal` or `-shm` left
  behind by another program can simply be deleted while nothing has the database open - or point
  `DB_PATH` somewhere else.
""")
p.write_text(s)
EOF

content.content:
NEW RESULT: spec-acceptance
Verdict for spec-acceptance: ACCEPT. Every requirement in SPEC.md sections 1-4 is met in the running app, and A1-A7 all pass on my own HTTP, database and browser checks. I have no findings this round. All five spec-acceptance findings from the last round are fixed.

Acceptance criteria:
- A1 Tenant isolation: PASS. Bob only ever sees West data in the list (also with q=EAST, tenant=East and tenantId=1), the export, operations, audit trail and courses. Every East detail id and an unknown id return 404 with byte-identical bodies. A cross-tenant revoke or roster request returns 404. A cross-tenant bulk issue on East courses 1, 2 and 3 returns 404, and a database snapshot taken before and after is identical row for row.
- A2 Retry safety: PASS. Five sequential replays returned the same body with Idempotent-Replayed: true. 30 concurrent identical requests on one key all returned 201 with a single distinct body (29 replayed). The database holds exactly one certificate and one certificate.issued audit event per eligible learner, one operation row per key, and no duplicate certificate for any learner and course.
- A3 Key misuse: PASS. Reusing the key with another course, an extra field, a string courseId or a third course gave 409 each time. The database was unchanged and the original body still replayed byte for byte. In a 24-request race between two payloads, one payload won (12 x 201, identical bodies), the other got 12 x 409, and only one operation was stored.
- A4 Learner outcomes: PASS. Safety 101 gives 2 issued and 3 skipped (already_certified, not_completed x2), each with a message. A second run issues 0. In the UI, a learner whose certificate was revoked is skipped with certificate_revoked.
- A5 Local dates: PASS. 2026-01-10T13:30:00Z shows as 2026-01-11 00:30 for East and 2026-01-10 21:30 for West, in the API, the list, the drawer, the CSV and the audit trail. The two DST-boundary certificates both show 02:30 local time (UTC+11 and UTC+10), which is correct. Sorted exports match an independent python zoneinfo oracle on local date, then instant, then id.
- A6 Export at scale: PASS. With 100,007 East certificates I ran 4 filtered and/or sorted exports, each twice, while list requests ran in parallel. Each took 1.3-1.9 s; the same full export takes about 0.23 s on an idle server. Each pair was byte-identical, and every file matched the python oracle row for row, with id as the tie-breaker (also in descending order). About 200 list requests per export were answered with no errors: median 13-20 ms, max 90 ms, against about 10 ms idle on a busy machine (load average 6). In the UI a list page loaded within 241 ms while a 100k export was downloading.
- A7 Revocation audit: PASS. A revoke returns alreadyRevoked=false and three repeats return true. 12 concurrent revokes of another certificate produced exactly one false. Exactly 2 new revocation audit events were written.

Other requirements:
- Startup: `PORT=7150 HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PATH=... npm start` installed, built the UI, created the demo data and served UI and API. It also worked from a pristine copy with no node_modules.
- Seed data: matches the spec and the README tables. Both tenants, zones and admins are present, and Safety 101 has completed, incomplete and already-certified enrollments.
- Generator: the seeded rows hash identically before and after generating, and again after --clear. The next serial number is still EAST-0000008 with the load-test data present.
- UI (Playwright, 41 checks, all workflows): everything works, including the actor switch at 360 px width after scrolling the top bar away. The one failed assertion was a mistake in my script, not in the app.
- Scope: no production auth, cloud deployment, notification or unrelated dependencies; the only runtime packages are express, better-sqlite3, react and react-dom.
- Last round's UI additions: none of them gets in the way of a workflow. The modal drawer and dialog make the top bar inert, but Escape or Close ends them. The course picker locks only while a bulk issue is in flight or its outcome is unknown, and is free again after a success. The status line reports the end of the run.

`npm test`: API 190 tests, 189 pass, 0 fail, 1 skipped; UI 252 of 252 pass; exit 0 in 81 s. The skipped test is the read-only-database one: user `nobody` cannot enter this machine's /tmp/claude-0 (mode 700). The README describes exactly this skip, so it is not a defect.

Clean-up: all servers I started (npm start, PID/PGID 9356; a fresh-copy npm start on port 7151; API servers with PIDs 25733 and the one in load.pid on ports 7152 and 7153) were stopped by PID or process group. Ports 7150-7155 no longer answer and no processes remain. I did not write outside /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/61a877e9-483e-575a-b7cf-c5b8e94decb9/scratchpad/final2/spec-acceptance.

然后这个是我对于作业的第六章的回答：1. Column Migration & Rollback
Why it fails: During a rolling deployment, old and new versions run at the same time. If you drop `display_name` too early, old instances crash because the column is missing. If you switch reads/writes to `full_name` before creating it, new instances crash. You also lose data and can't safely roll back once `display_name` is dropped.
Safe sequence:

1. Add `full_name` as nullable in the database.
2. Deploy code that writes to both `display_name` and `full_name`, while still reading from `display_name`.
3. Backfill existing `display_name` values into `full_name` in small batches.
4. Deploy code that reads from `full_name` (falling back to `display_name` if null) while keeping dual-writes on.
5. Once confident and no rollback is needed, stop writing to `display_name`.
6. In a later release, drop `display_name`.

2. Stale Cache After Revocation
Why a 5-second TTL doesn't fix it: It doesn't remove the race condition—it just shrinks the window where bad data is served. Even for 5 seconds, a revoked certificate could still look `ACTIVE` to callers, which is a security bug.
How to fix it:

* Version check (best): Give each certificate a monotonically increasing `version` number. When B revokes it, bump the version in the DB and write a `REVOKED` entry (or tombstone) with that new version to the cache. When A tries to write back to the cache, only let the write succeed if A's version is newer than what's already in the cache.
* Locking alternative: Use a per-certificate lock around cache updates/deletes so A's read-and-populate and B's revoke-and-invalidate can't interleave out of order.

3. Cascading Failure & Recovery
Chain of failure: Normally, 1,000 req/s at 20 ms takes about 20 workers. When B slows to 2 seconds, requests hit the 100 ms timeout and retry up to 3 times—turning 1,000 req/s into up to 4,000 calls against B and holding each request open longer. All 50 workers on A get tied up waiting on `/report`, starving every other endpoint on A.
How to fix `/report`:

* Isolate resources: Cap how many workers `/report` (or calls to B) can use at once so other endpoints still have free workers.
* Add a circuit breaker: If B times out or errors too often, trip the circuit breaker and fail fast without calling B until it recovers.
* Cut back retries: Drop aggressive retries when B is struggling (or use a tight retry budget) so you don't flood a slow service.

What `/report` should return when B is unhealthy: Return a fast degraded response—like a cached report if you have one (ideally marked stale), or a quick `503 Service Unavailable` with a `Retry-After` header (or `202 Accepted` if queued for async processing).  然后他的题目是：Answer all three questions in written-answers.md , in your own words. 
1. A service stores user names in users.display_name. A proposed release introduces
users.full_name, changes all application reads and writes to the new column, and drops
display_name in the same deployment. The service uses rolling deployment, so old and new
application instances run concurrently. The release must also support rollback. Explain why
this release can fail and propose a safe sequence of database and application changes.
2. Certificate details are cached for 60 seconds. Request A misses the cache and reads ACTIVE
from the database. Before A writes to the cache, request B revokes the certificate, commits
the database transaction, and deletes the cache entry. A then writes its stale ACTIVE value
into the cache. A colleague proposes reducing the cache TTL to five seconds. Explain why this
does not fix the problem. Redesign the read and revocation paths so that any read starting
after B returns success cannot receive the stale ACTIVE value.
3. Service A has 50 request workers. Every request to its /report endpoint calls Service B with a
100 ms timeout and up to three retries. Traffic to /report remains at 1,000 requests per
second. B's latency suddenly rises from 20 ms to 2 seconds, and unrelated endpoints on A
soon stop responding. Explain the chain of failure, including the effect of retries. Redesign
/report so unrelated endpoints remain available, and state what /report should return when
B is unhealthy 你看看我回答的怎么样

content.content:
NEW RESULT: test-quality
On the whole the suites can be trusted. Every reliability run I made was green, and the one exception is a single UI test that flakes. "npm test" ran green 3 times on Node 22 (62, 68 and 69 s), once on Node 20 (79 s) and once on Node 24 (67 s), so the README's "about a minute" holds. It also passed with the hostile settings exported (63 s) and with TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati LANG=de_DE. The backend suite passed 3 times under 4 busy loops plus other load (61-62 s at load average about 9). Response times in those runs stayed far below the limits the tests assert (slowest list request 62 ms against a 1-2 s limit). It also passed with SQLITE_DRIVER=node, and I confirmed that node:sqlite was really the driver used. The UI suite passed 10 times in a row (8-11 s each) and under 10 shuffled seeds. Each of the 9 UI files passes alone, and each of the 190 backend tests passes alone. The counts match the README (190 API tests, 252 UI tests).

Mutation spot check, 69 mutants: all 25 frontend mutants and 39 of 44 backend mutants were caught. The round-4 fixes are all guarded by tests. Removing the rosterOutdated part of canIssue in BulkIssuePage.jsx fails the "stays locked ..." test every time (20 of 20 runs). The 100 runs of that test under load were deterministic. In real Chromium, 291 scripted clicks sent exactly one POST. I compared the dialog Tab trap, inert background and in-flight lock, and the --topbar-height value (70px sticky, 0px at 360 px width), with Playwright: the browser behaves as the simulated-DOM tests claim. Re-recording frontend/test/fixtures/recorded.json changed only timestamps and serials, so the fixtures have not drifted from what the backend sends.

The verification command is honest:
- A failing backend mutant makes npm test exit 1 without running the UI suite.
- A failing UI mutant makes it exit 1.
- A test file that crashes on import fails the run, both in the backend and in the UI.
- A handler that never answers is reported by test name after 60 s; the run ends in 241 s with exit 1.
- Even a leaked export slot, which hangs about 26 tests, ends in 921 s with every test named.
- No world-writable directories are left behind. Ctrl+C or SIGTERM of the runner cleans up its temp dirs.
- With a private TMPDIR, nothing is left except Node's own node-compile-cache.
- The repository matches the manifest and has no extra files after all runs; data/ is untouched.

What does not hold:
- (1) The read-only database test is skipped when the suite runs as root from this hand-over location, and its skip message gives the wrong reason. Removing assertWritable() from bootstrap.js then goes unnoticed. In a copy that "nobody" can read, the test runs and catches that mutant. The whole backend suite run as nobody passes 190 of 190 with nothing skipped.
- (2) One UI test, "gives the page back when a deep link is left with both dialogs open", is flaky under load (2 of 100 runs failed). The cause is a race in the test, not in the product.
- (3) The CSV formula-injection triggers tab and CR are not tested.
- (4) The tolerance for a directory that already exists in createDirectory is not tested (nit).

Mutants I judged equivalent:
- R02 (download.js reports the stream error instead of the source failure): equivalent on Node 22 and 24, caught on Node 20.
- A02 (no tenant filter on a certificate's audit events): certificate ids are global, and the certificate row is already checked against the tenant.
- A09 (sort by the UTC instant instead of the local date): within one time zone the order is the same. It was caught only because it is slow.

Clean-up: every process I started has stopped (the servers on 7001 and 7002, the 4 busy loops, the loops and the mutation scripts). No port in 7000-7049 is listening, and the copies under /tmp/tq-test-quality-* are removed. The 30-minute wait loop I left running in the background (it only polled a log file) was stopped by its time limit; nothing else is left over. All logs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/61a877e9-483e-575a-b7cf-c5b8e94decb9/scratchpad/final2/test-quality/.
